intro: Landscapes can become shorthand for a nation. Compare what each scene chooses to see and how a painter's brushwork or viewpoint can make that choice feel natural.
alt: Four regional landscape studies show a northern lake, an Australian bush track, colorful Brazilian hills and an Andean scene with figures.

variants.name: Group of Seven
variants.look: Bright orange foliage and rugged rock stand out against a deep blue northern lake.
variants.history: The Group of Seven formed in Canada in 1920. Its members made distinctive landscapes and took part in debates about national art.
variants.when: Study how close colors and bold brush marks can distill a large rocky view.
variants.why: Strong simplification makes an individual site easy to recognize and adapt into a broader story about a region.

variants.name: Heidelberg School
variants.look: Sunlit grasses and eucalypts are described with broken dabs and light shadows along the path.
variants.history: Late nineteenth-century Australian artists associated with the Heidelberg School worked outdoors and developed styles also described as Australian Impressionism.
variants.when: Study how quick brush marks record the distinctive light on a local landscape.
variants.why: Broken color and pale values can suggest bright sun without describing every leaf or blade of grass.

variants.name: Brazilian Modernism
variants.look: Rounded blocks and bold colors simplify a landscape of urban hills and tropical plants.
variants.history: Brazilian modernism took many forms. São Paulo's Modern Art Week of 1922 was a watershed, and artists such as Tarsila do Amaral developed distinctive modern compositions from Brazilian places and imagery.
variants.when: Study the way specific vegetation, city forms and colors retain a local character as shapes become more abstract.
variants.why: Simplification lets the subject support new formal invention while keeping a strong sense of place.

variants.name: Indigenismo
variants.look: People, buildings and the slope of the land share an earth-toned structure in the Andes-inspired scene.
variants.history: Twentieth-century Indigenismo in Latin America encompassed distinct movements. In Peru, José Sabogal made Indigenous subjects central to a national art debate, raising questions about who could represent whose experience.
variants.when: Study who painted the work, its audience and the position of the people depicted.
variants.why: An image can give a public role to people and places previously ignored while still carrying the maker's viewpoint.

source.label: ICAA at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston
